claim: Cell-specific chromatin accessibility data can be produced via ectopic expression of E. coli Dam methylase in vivo, without the requirement for cell-sorting (CATaDa).
source: Here we show that cell-specific chromatin accessibility data can be produced via ectopic expression of E. coli Dam methylase in vivo, without the requirement for cell-sorting (CATaDa).
evidence: The abstract directly states this as a main finding of the study, and the manuscript presents experimental data supporting this claim throughout.

claim: Chromatin accessibility profiles produced with CATaDa in the eye disc were highly reproducible between replicates (r2 = 0.947).
source: Chromatin accessibility profiles produced with CATaDa in the eye disc were highly reproducible between replicates (r2 = 0.947) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific correlation coefficient value and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing correlation plots.

claim: CATaDa profiles showed good agreement with data produced with ATAC-seq and FAIRE-seq.
source: CATaDa profiles showed good agreement with data produced with ATAC-seq and FAIRE-seq.
evidence: The manuscript presents visual inspection data and quantitative comparisons between CATaDa and other methods.

claim: Open chromatin is enriched at transcriptional start sites (TSS) in CATaDa profiles.
source: For example, open chromatin is enriched at transcriptional start sites (TSS) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows an aggregation plot demonstrating enrichment at TSS.

claim: The overlap of Dam identified peaks with ATAC and FAIRE peaks is 48.6% and 49.4%, respectively.
source: The overlap of Dam identified peaks with ATAC and FAIRE peaks is 48.6% and 49.4%, respectively (In comparison, 55.9% of ATAC peaks are also identified in FAIRE data – Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of peak overlap between methods.

claim: The overlap between CATaDa and ATAC peaks is highly significant (p<1 × 10−5).
source: A Monte Carlo simulation determined that this is a highly significant overlap (p<1 × 10−5) and peak heights at shared ATAC and CATaDa peaks show significant correlation (p<1 × 10-16, r2 = 0.138) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Monte Carlo simulation was performed to assess statistical significance of the overlap.

claim: CATaDa identified 57.9% of FlyLight eye enhancers (333 of 575 enhancers).
source: We found that for 57.9% of FlyLight eye enhancers, a corresponding peak was called in CATaDa profiles (333 of 575 enhancers).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of validated enhancers identified by CATaDa.

claim: In Drosophila, neurons are derived from asymmetrically dividing neural stem cells (NSCs).
source: In Drosophila, neurons are derived from asymmetrically dividing neural stem cells (NSCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neurogenesis.

claim: NSC divisions produce one self-renewing daughter NSC and a ganglion mother cell (GMC), which divides once more to produce neurons or glia.
source: NSC divisions produce one self-renewing daughter NSC and a ganglion mother cell (GMC), which divides once more to produce neurons or glia (Homem and Knoblich, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Homem and Knoblich, 2012.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of differentially accessible regions in CNS lineages indicates two major groupings in which chromatin is most accessible in either stem cells or mature neurons.
source: Hierarchical clustering of regions of chromatin with differential accessibility between cell types reveals two major clusters in which chromatin is either open in stem cells but inaccessible in neurons, or vice versa (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows hierarchical clustering results demonstrating these two major groups.

claim: The E-box motif – CAGCNG – which is bound by the NSC proneural factor ase was highly enriched in regions of open chromatin in NSCs.
source: Identification of enriched motifs in sequences that were accessible in NSCs showed that expected transcription factor binding sites were highly enriched. For example, the E-box motif – CAGCNG – which is bound by the NSC proneural factor ase (Figure 4D) (Southall and Brand, 2009; Jarman et al., 1993).
evidence: Motif analysis identified this sequence in NSC-accessible regions, supported by citations.

claim: Regions in which open chromatin was specifically enriched in mature neurons yielded a sequence motif corresponding to the transcription factor, Ci.
source: Regions in which open chromatin was specifically enriched in mature neurons yielded a sequence motif corresponding to the transcription factor, Ci.
evidence: Motif analysis of neuron-specific accessible regions identified Ci binding motifs.

claim: The Drosophila midgut contains a pool of cycling intestinal stem cells (ISCs) that persists in the adult to maintain a population of terminally differentiated cells.
source: The Drosophila midgut contains a pool of cycling intestinal stem cells (ISCs) that persists in the adult to maintain a population of terminally differentiated cells which mediate the absorptive and secretory functions of the organ (Jiang and Edgar, 2011; Nászai et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jiang and Edgar, 2011 and Nászai et al., 2015.

claim: A single committed immature progenitor cell (enteroblast – EB) is produced from stem cell divisions, which then differentiates without further divisions to produce the mature epithelial cells of the midgut.
source: In contrast to neurogenesis, a single committed immature progenitor cell (enteroblast – EB) is produced from stem cell divisions, which then differentiates without further divisions to produce the mature epithelial cells of the midgut (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007.

claim: escargot (esg) is a transcription factor required for ISC self-renewal.
source: For example, escargot (esg) a transcription factor required for ISC self-renewal (Korzelius et al., 2014), displays multiple peaks of accessible chromatin at the gene body and surrounding region in ISCs and EBs, whilst little signal is observed in the ECs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Korzelius et al., 2014.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of differentially accessible regions in gut cell types revealed two major groups in which accessible chromatin was enriched in either in the stem cells (ISCs) or differentiated cell (ECs).
source: As observed in the CNS, hierarchical clustering revealed two major groups in which accessible chromatin was enriched in either in the stem cells (ISCs) or differentiated cell (ECs) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows hierarchical clustering results for midgut cell types.

claim: Principal component analysis reveals two distinct clusters in which >80% of the variance is explained in the first two principal components, representing the two distinct tissue types (CNS and midgut).
source: Principal component analysis reveals two distinct clusters in which >80% of the variance is explained in the first two principal components (Figure 5E). These clusters represent the two distinct tissue types, (CNS and midgut) rather than immature and differentiated cells.
evidence: Figure 5E shows PCA results demonstrating tissue-specific clustering.

claim: The greatest correlation outside of a lineage was between the two stem cell types (R2 = 0.76).
source: Interestingly, the greatest correlation outside of a lineage was between the two stem cell types (R2 = 0.76), whilst differentiated cells exhibited only weak correlation (ISCs vs NSC, R2 = 0.51).
evidence: Correlation analysis between cell types across lineages shows highest similarity between stem cells.

claim: Somatic stem cell types may utilise a broadly similar chromatin landscape for the maintenance of multipotency, whilst lineage-specific variation is relatively small.
source: This indicates that somatic stem cell types may utilise a broadly similar chromatin landscape for the maintenance of multipotency, whilst lineage-specific variation is relatively small.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data showing high similarity between NSCs and ISCs.

claim: 17 of 30 lines (57%) tested showed GFP expression in tissues and cell types that closely matched predictions based on CATaDa data.
source: Overall 17 of 30 lines (57%) tested showed GFP expression in tissues and cell types that closely matched our predictions based on CATaDa data.
evidence: The manuscript reports the success rate of enhancer prediction validation experiments.

claim: The 57% enhancer prediction rate is in line with the rate of enhancer prediction by previous methods.
source: This is in line with the rate of enhancer prediction by previous methods (Kvon et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript compares its enhancer prediction success rate to previously published methods.

claim: Differentiated neurons had fewer GATC fragments with lower read counts compared to NSCs.
source: Initial examination of read distributions indicated that differentiated neurons had fewer GATC fragments with lower read counts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1A shows read distribution data comparing neurons and NSCs.

claim: There was a significantly greater proportion of GATC fragments with low read counts but without being completely inaccessible (~1–3 rpm), in the NSC data compared to neurons.
source: We observed that there was a significantly greater proportion of GATC fragments with low read counts but without being completely inaccessible (~1–3 rpm), in the NSC data compared to neurons (Figure 7A).
evidence: Figure 7A shows distribution plots demonstrating this difference between NSCs and neurons.

claim: This abundance of genomic regions in the stem cells with low-level chromatin accessibility indicates that open chromatin is more broadly distributed than in NSCs than neurons.
source: This abundance of genomic regions in the stem cells with low-level chromatin accessibility indicates that open chromatin is more broadly distributed than in NSCs than neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the read distribution data showing more low-accessibility regions in NSCs.

claim: There was a trend towards greater number of GATC fragments to which zero reads were mapped as differentiation progresses.
source: Conversely, we observed a trend towards greater number of GATC fragments to which zero reads were mapped as differentiation progresses (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1B shows data on regions with zero mapped reads across cell types.

claim: Global changes to accessible chromatin are a common feature of somatic stem cell lineages in vivo.
source: These trends are also observed in the midgut cells, implying that global changes to accessible chromatin are a common feature of somatic stem cell lineages in vivo (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript shows similar trends in both CNS and midgut lineages, supporting this generalization.

claim: Chromatin is highly accessible in pluripotent cell types such as embryonic stem (ES) cells, but is compacted following differentiation.
source: Chromatin is highly accessible in pluripotent cell types such as embryonic stem (ES) cells, but is compacted following differentiation (Meshorer and Misteli, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Meshorer and Misteli, 2006.

claim: It has been suggested that open chromatin in pluripotent cells represents a permissive state to which multiple programmes of gene regulation may be rapidly applied upon differentiation.
source: It has been suggested that this open chromatin represents a permissive state to which multiple programmes of gene regulation may be rapidly applied upon differentiation (Gaspar-Maia et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gaspar-Maia et al., 2011.

claim: Ectopic expression of untethered DNA adenine methyltransferase (Dam) results in specific methylation of open chromatin regions whilst nucleosome bound DNA is protected.
source: It has been suggested that ectopic expression of untethered DNA adenine methyltransferase (Dam) results in specific methylation of open chromatin regions whilst nucleosome bound DNA is protected (Wines et al., 1996; Bulanenkova et al., 2007; Boivin and Dura, 1998; Singh and Klar, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Transgenic expression of fusions of Dam to DNA-binding proteins is a well-established method used to assess transcription factor occupancy (DNA adenine methyltransferase identification - DamID).
source: Transgenic expression of fusions of Dam to DNA-binding proteins is a well-established method used to assess transcription factor occupancy (DNA adenine methyltransferase identification - DamID) (van Steensel and Henikoff, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to van Steensel and Henikoff, 2000.

claim: DamID can be adapted to profile DNA-protein interactions in a cell-type-specific manner by utilising ribosome re-initiation to attenuate transgene expression.
source: Recently, it was demonstrated that DamID could be adapted to profile DNA-protein interactions in a cell-type-specific manner by utilising ribosome re-initiation to attenuate transgene expression (Marshall et al., 2016; Aughey and Southall, 2016; Southall et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2016; Aughey and Southall, 2016; Southall et al., 2013.

claim: CATaDa signal frequency increases dramatically towards the centre of ATAC or FAIRE peaks.
source: We observe that CATaDa signal frequency increases dramatically towards the centre of ATAC or FAIRE peaks (Figure 2D).
evidence: Figure 2D shows aggregation plots demonstrating enrichment of CATaDa signal at ATAC and FAIRE peaks.

claim: For peaks identified in either ATAC or FAIRE data that are not present in CATaDa, there is a relative lack of GATC motifs.
source: We also observe that for peaks identified in either ATAC or FAIRE data that are not present in CATaDa, there is a relative lack of GATC motifs, which suggests that there may be cases in which false negatives are observed due to the limitations of the resolution achievable by Dam methylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B shows GATC frequency at peaks identified by different methods.

claim: CATaDa identified fewer peaks than FAIRE in regions proximal to gene promoters (when compared with ATAC).
source: We found that whilst CATaDa identified fewer peaks than FAIRE in regions proximal to gene promoters (when compared with ATAC), CATaDa was notably better at identification of non-promoter adjacent accessible sites in ATAC data compared to FAIRE-seq (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows comparison of peak identification at different genomic features.

claim: The lack of promoter peaks identified can be explained by the relative depletion of GATC sites upstream of TSS.
source: The lack of promoter peaks identified can again be explained by the relative depletion of GATC sites upstream of TSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3C shows GATC frequency around TSS.

claim: bruchpilot (brp) is specifically transcribed in neurons and has an important role in synapse function.
source: This corresponds with the expression of brp, which is specifically transcribed in neurons and has an important role in synapse function (Wagh et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wagh et al., 2006.

claim: Wnt signalling is known to be important for the control of stem cell populations.
source: Wnt signalling is known to be important for the control of stem cell populations, therefore, these results are also expected (Ring et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ring et al., 2014.

claim: Open chromatin is still detectable in GMCs/newly born neurons at NSC-specific gene loci, indicating that functional elements required for regulation of NSC gene expression are not immediately rendered inaccessible following differentiation.
source: Interestingly, open chromatin is still detectable in these regions in the GMCs/newly born neurons. This pattern is also observed with other NSC expressed factors such as deadpan (dpn), CyclinE (CycE) and prospero (pros) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Furthermore, GMC/newly born neuron profiles frequently show intermediate signal at these loci, indicating that functional elements required for regulation of NSC gene expression are not immediately rendered inaccessible following differentiation (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing intermediate accessibility in GMCs/newly born neurons at NSC gene loci.

claim: There are a large number of loci that are inaccessible in NSCs, then open in the intermediate GMCs/newly born neurons stage before being rendered inaccessible again in terminally differentiated neurons.
source: There are a large number of loci that are inaccessible in NSCs, then open in the intermediate GMCs/newly born neurons stage before being rendered inaccessible again in terminally differentiated neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows hierarchical clustering revealing this pattern of accessibility.

claim: A cluster enriched in larval neurons demonstrates that the chromatin accessibility landscape of larval neurons, although similar, is distinct from adult neurons.
source: In addition, a cluster enriched in larval neurons demonstrates that the chromatin accessibility landscape of larval neurons, although similar, is distinct from adult neurons.
evidence: Hierarchical clustering analysis shows distinct patterns for larval versus adult neurons.

claim: Chromatin accessibility in intermediate cell types is broadly more similar to their stem cell precursors than their differentiated progeny in CNS and midgut lineages.
source: Interestingly, we observe that chromatin accessibility in intermediate cell types is broadly more similar to their stem cell precursors than their differentiated progeny in CNS and midgut lineages (Figure 4B,C, Figure 5B,C,F).
evidence: Correlation and clustering analyses show this relationship between cell types.

claim: Many stem-cell-specific regulatory regions remain accessible in intermediate cell types and are not fully repressed until terminal differentiation.
source: This indicates that many stem-cell-specific regulatory regions remain accessible in intermediate cell types and are not fully repressed until terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that intermediate cells show accessibility patterns more similar to stem cells.

claim: Immature post-mitotic neurons have been experimentally induced to dedifferentiate by interventions that are ineffective in fully differentiated adult cells.
source: This idea is supported by the fact that immature post-mitotic neurons have been experimentally induced to dedifferentiate by interventions that are ineffective in fully differentiated adult cells (Southall et al., 2014; Marshall and Brand, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Southall et al., 2014 and Marshall and Brand, 2017.

claim: In some physiological contexts differentiated cells may revert to replenish stem cell pools.
source: It has been suggested that in some physiological contexts differentiated cells may revert to replenish stem cell pools (Kai and Spradling, 2004; Yan et al., 2017; Cheetham and Brand, 2018; Jin et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: NSCs in the developing Drosophila CNS appear to have more broadly open chromatin landscapes than their fully differentiated progeny.
source: With CATaDa we have acquired evidence to indicate that NSCs in the developing Drosophila CNS appear to have more broadly open chromatin landscapes than their fully differentiated progeny.
evidence: Read distribution analysis shows NSCs have more regions with low-level accessibility than neurons.

claim: The intermediate or immature progenitors, in both the CNS and midgut, retain a relatively open chromatin state, similar to that of their stem cell precursors.
source: Furthermore, the intermediate or immature progenitors, in both the CNS and midgut, retain a relatively open chromatin state, similar to that of their stem cell precursors (Figure 4B–C, Figure 5B,D,F).
evidence: Data from both lineages show intermediate cells have accessibility patterns similar to stem cells.

claim: In pluripotent stem cells, the more highly accessible chromatin landscape is thought to promote rapid initiation of multiple gene expression programmes.
source: In pluripotent stem cells, the more highly accessible chromatin landscape is thought to promote rapid initiation of multiple gene expression programmes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pluripotent stem cells.

claim: The fact that broadly accessible chromatin is also a feature of somatic stem cells suggests that these cells may retain an unexpected level of plasticity even after their terminal cell fate has been specified.
source: The fact that this is also a feature of somatic stem cells suggests that these cells may retain an unexpected level of plasticity even after their terminal cell fate has been specified.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that somatic stem cells have broadly accessible chromatin like pluripotent cells.

claim: CATaDa yields chromatin accessibility profiles for defined cell types in vivo without the need for cell isolation, fixation or the extraction of naked chromatin.
source: We have demonstrated that CATaDa yields chromatin accessibility profiles for defined cell types in vivo without the need for cell isolation, fixation or the extraction of naked chromatin.
evidence: The manuscript describes the method and demonstrates its application without these requirements.

claim: The marking of accessible DNA occurs in vivo in CATaDa, so there are no artefacts associated with chemical fixation or washing of the chromatin prior to the assay.
source: In addition to its ease of use, CATaDa also has the advantage that the marking of accessible DNA occurs in vivo. Due to this, there are no artefacts associated with chemical fixation or washing of the chromatin prior to the assay (Baranello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the method design, supported by a citation about fixation artifacts.

claim: Widely used tissue dissociation protocols have recently been shown to result in substantial gene expression artefacts.
source: Furthermore, widely used tissue dissociation protocols have recently been shown to result in substantial gene expression artefacts, a risk that is also circumvented by labelling the DNA in vivo (van den Brink et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to van den Brink et al., 2017.

claim: As Dam is expressed in vivo over several hours, the profiles produced will reflect dynamic changes to chromatin structure over the entire time period during which Dam is expressed.
source: In addition, as Dam is expressed in vivo over several hours, the profiles produced will reflect dynamic changes to chromatin structure over the entire time period during which Dam is expressed.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design where Dam is expressed over time.

claim: CATaDa is limited by its resolution, which is restricted by the frequency of GATC sites in the genome (median spacing of ~200 bp in Drosophila).
source: CATaDa is limited by its resolution, which is restricted by the frequency of GATC sites in the genome (median spacing of ~200 bp in Drosophila).
evidence: This is a known limitation based on the mechanism of Dam methylation.

claim: The resolution of CATaDa can be increased by using a modified Dam in conjunction with immunoprecipitation (Dam-IP).
source: However, this can be increased by using a modified Dam in conjunction with immunoprecipitation (Dam-IP)(Xiao et al., 2010; Xiao and Moore, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2010 and Xiao and Moore, 2011.

claim: Extensive sequence biases have been reported for DNAse and ATAC-seq.
source: It is worth noting that extensive sequence biases have also been reported for DNAse and ATAC-seq (Madrigal, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Madrigal, 2015.

claim: For FAIRE-seq it is recommended to have a minimum of 1 × 106 cells.
source: For example, for FAIRE-seq it is recommended to have a minimum of 1 × 106 cells (Tsompana and Buck, 2014; Simon et al., 2013), whilst DNase-seq typically requires 1 × 107 cells (Tsompana and Buck, 2014; Song and Crawford, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published protocols.

claim: DamID experiments can be performed with as few as 1000 cells.
source: In contrast, DamID experiments can be performed with as few as 1000 cells (Tosti, 2017), therefore CATaDa is likely to also be effective with low cell numbers, making it competitive with ATAC-seq (500–50,000 cells) (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Marshall et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tosti, 2017 and other studies.

claim: Single cell DamID has been demonstrated, indicating that the minimum number of cells required for CATaDa is one.
source: Furthermore, single cell DamID has also recently been demonstrated, indicating that the minimum number of cells required for CATaDa is one (Kind et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kind et al., 2015.

claim: Dam methylase is a relatively small protein compared to Tn5 transposase (55 and 32 KDa respectively).
source: This could be accounted for by the fact that Dam methylase is a relatively small protein compared to Tn5 transposase (utilised in ATAC-seq – 55 and 32 KDa respectively [Naumann and Reznikoff, 2002; Boye et al., 1992]), Therefore, Dam may be able to methylate sites which are inaccessible to Tn5.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations providing the molecular weights of these proteins.

claim: Dam may be able to methylate some nucleosome bound DNA in which the GATC site is exposed to the nucleoplasm, which may be insufficient for transposition.
source: Alternatively, Dam may be able to methylate some nucleosome bound DNA in which the GATC site is exposed to the nucleoplasm, which may be insufficient for transposition.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between CATaDa and ATAC-seq results.

claim: Targeted DamID is rapidly being embraced by the Drosophila community with, at present, over 135 laboratories having requested the reagents.
source: Targeted DamID is rapidly being embraced by the Drosophila community with, at present, over 135 laboratories having requested the reagents and a number of papers already published (Southall et al., 2013; Dinges et al., 2017; Marshall and Brand, 2017; Cheetham and Brand, 2018; Jin et al., 2015b; Spéder and Brand, 2018).
evidence: This statement provides a specific number and is supported by citations to published papers using the technique.

claim: Progress is being made in adapting Targeted DamID for use in vertebrate models.
source: Progress is also being made in adapting it for use in vertebrate models (Tosti, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tosti, 2017.

claim: Whenever the binding of a protein of interest (POI) is investigated with Targeted DamID, Dam-only data (representing chromatin accessibility) for the cell type being assayed is also generated, as it is the control for which the Dam-POI is normalised.
source: Whenever the binding of a protein of interest (POI) is investigated with this technique, Dam-only data (representing chromatin accessibility) for the cell type being assayed is also generated, as it is the control for which the Dam-POI is normalised.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental design of DamID experiments.

claim: Regions that are bound by transcription factors that activate transcription may be replaced by transcriptional repressors in stem cell progeny.
source: Firstly, regions that are bound by transcription factors that activate transcription may be replaced by transcriptional repressors.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why some regions remain accessible in intermediate cells.

claim: Repressive factors are known to have detectable open chromatin 'footprints', similarly to activating factors.
source: Such repressive factors are known to have detectable open chromatin 'footprints', similarly to activating factors (Mall et al., 2017; Dinges et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mall et al., 2017 and Dinges et al., 2017.

claim: Retention of open chromatin regions in intermediate cell types may reflect increased plasticity, indicating that cell fate has not yet been fully determined and that lineage reversion or dedifferentiation is possible given the introduction of the correct combination of factors.
source: Retention of open chromatin regions in intermediate cell types may also reflect increased plasticity, indicating that cell fate has not yet been fully determined and that lineage reversion or dedifferentiation is possible given the introduction of the correct combination of factors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed chromatin accessibility patterns.
